A physical quantity is anything we can measure, and every measurement has two parts: a number and a unit. "The table is 1.5" means nothing; "the table is $1.5\,\mathrm{m}$ long" is a measurement.

SI base units

Scientists everywhere use the International System of Units (SI). It starts from seven base quantities:

⟦0⟧

Every other unit is a derived unit built from these. Speed is distance divided by time, so its unit is $\mathrm{m/s}$. Force is mass times acceleration, so $1\,\mathrm{N} = 1\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2}$. Energy is force times distance, so $1\,\mathrm{J} = 1\,\mathrm{N\,m} = 1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s^2}$.

Prefixes

Prefixes scale a unit up or down by powers of ten:

⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧

Squared and cubed units

A square metre is a square $100\,\mathrm{cm}$ on each side, so $1\,\mathrm{m^2} = 100 \times 100 = 10\,000\,\mathrm{cm^2}$. For volumes the factor is cubed: $1\,\mathrm{m^3} = 1\,000\,000\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. Also $1\,\mathrm{L} = 1000\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and $1\,\mathrm{m^3} = 1000\,\mathrm{L}$.

⟦4⟧

Speeds: km/h and m/s

⟦5⟧

So divide by 3.6 to go from km/h to m/s, and multiply by 3.6 to go back: $72\,\mathrm{km/h} = 20\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Scientific notation

Very large and very small numbers are written as $a \times 10^n$ with $1 \le a \lt 10$. The speed of light is $3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$; the charge of an electron is $1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. In a calculator or on this site you can type these as 3e8 and 1.6e-19.

No measurement is perfectly exact. A good measurement says how big something is and how precisely we know it.

Instruments and their precision

⟦0⟧

Reading a vernier caliper

Read the main scale just to the left of the vernier zero, then find the vernier line that lines up exactly with a main-scale line. With 10 vernier divisions, that line number gives tenths of a millimetre.

⟦1⟧

Reading a micrometer

The sleeve shows whole and half millimetres; the thimble has 50 divisions of $0.01\,\mathrm{mm}$. Reading = sleeve + thimble $\times\ 0.01\,\mathrm{mm}$. A sleeve showing $5.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ with thimble line 23 gives $5.5 + 0.23 = 5.73\,\mathrm{mm}$.

Uncertainty

A single reading is usually quoted with an uncertainty of about half the smallest division, for example $12.5 \pm 0.05\,\mathrm{cm}$ on a millimetre ruler. For several readings of the same quantity, use the mean as the best value and let the spread of the readings show the uncertainty.

⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧

Calculating with measurements

  • Multiplying or dividing: give the answer to the fewest significant figures of the values used. $12.5\,\mathrm{cm} \times 3.2\,\mathrm{cm} = 40.0 \to 40\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ (2 s.f.).
  • Adding or subtracting: give the answer to the fewest decimal places. $12.52 + 3.1 = 15.62 \to 15.6$.

To add vectors, place them head to tail; the resultant runs from the first tail to the last head.

⟦1⟧

⟦3⟧

Stress $\sigma$ is force per area (in $\mathrm{Pa}$); strain $\varepsilon$ is the fractional change in length (no unit). The Young's modulus $E$ is a property of the material, not of the particular wire: steel has about $2 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

An object oscillates in simple harmonic motion (SHM) when the force pulling it back to its rest position is proportional to how far it has been moved: $F = -kx$. A mass on a spring and a pendulum swinging through small angles are the classic examples.

  • Amplitude $A$: the largest displacement from the rest position.
  • Period $T$: the time for one complete oscillation; frequency $f = 1/T$; angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$.
  • The displacement follows a sine or cosine curve: $x = A\cos(\omega t)$.
⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧

Speed, acceleration and energy

  • The speed is greatest at the centre: $v_{\max} = A\omega$. At displacement $x$: $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$.

⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧

Plane mirrors

The image in a flat mirror is virtual (the light only seems to come from it), upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted (left and right swapped) and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Two mirrors at an angle $\alpha$ form $n = \dfrac{360^\circ}{\alpha} - 1$ images.

A concave mirror (curved inwards, like the inside of a spoon) brings parallel rays together at its focal point F. A convex mirror (curved outwards) spreads them out as if they came from a focal point behind it. The focal length is half the radius of curvature, $f = \frac{R}{2}$.

When two waves meet they add up (superposition). If crest meets crest they reinforce: constructive interference. If crest meets trough they cancel: destructive interference. To see a steady pattern the sources must be coherent: the same frequency and a constant phase difference.

Young's double slit

Light through two narrow slits a distance $d$ apart makes bright and dark fringes on a screen a distance $L$ away. For small angles:

⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧

Diffraction

Waves spread out when they pass through a gap. For a single slit of width $a$ the dark fringes are at $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$, and the central bright band is twice as wide as the others. A diffraction grating has very many slits, $N$ per unit length, so the slit spacing is $d = 1/N$. Its bright lines are sharp and obey $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$; the highest order that can appear is the largest whole number below $d/\lambda$.

The colours of soap bubbles and oil films come from thin-film interference between light reflected from the top and the bottom of the film.

Einstein built special relativity (1905) on two postulates:

  1. The laws of physics are the same in every inertial (non-accelerating) frame of reference.
  2. The speed of light in a vacuum, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, is the same for every observer, however fast they or the source move.

Accepting both means that time and length depend on the observer. Everything is controlled by the Lorentz factor

⟦0⟧

⟦4⟧

which never exceeds $c$.

Mass is a form of energy. An object of mass $m$ at rest has rest energy $E_0 = mc^2$, and its total energy when moving is $E = \gamma mc^2$, so its kinetic energy is $E_k = (\gamma - 1)mc^2$.

Light carries energy in tiny packets called photons. Planck and Einstein showed that the energy of one photon depends only on its frequency:

⟦0⟧

with Planck's constant $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$. Photon energies are tiny, so they are often given in electronvolts: $1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, the energy an electron gains across $1\,\mathrm{V}$.

The photoelectric effect

Light shining on a clean metal can knock electrons out of it. The experiments showed:

⟦1⟧
  • below a threshold frequency $f_0$ no electrons come out, however bright the light;
  • above it, electrons come out at once, and their maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency, not the brightness;
  • brighter light gives more electrons, not faster ones.
⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧

Matter waves

De Broglie suggested that particles also behave as waves, with wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$. Electron diffraction confirmed it, and electron microscopes use it to see details far smaller than light can.

Fission

A slow neutron absorbed by uranium-235 makes it split into two smaller nuclei and 2 or 3 new neutrons, releasing about $200\,\mathrm{MeV}$. The new neutrons can split further nuclei: a chain reaction. In a reactor:

  • the moderator (water or graphite) slows the neutrons so that they cause fission more easily;
  • control rods (boron or cadmium) absorb neutrons so that, on average, each fission causes exactly one more;
  • the coolant carries the heat to make steam for the turbines;
  • thick concrete shielding absorbs the radiation.

Fusion

In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium at about 15 million kelvin; only at such temperatures do nuclei move fast enough to overcome their electric repulsion. Fusion fuel is plentiful and leaves little long-lived waste, but a practical fusion power station has not yet been built.
